set.description: Mara's father, currently in London while the municipal archive remains closed after the eastern flood-barrier alert. He wants to protect Mara and preserve records without provoking authorities, and knows Mara has signed an agreement to write for the Continuance Project and has learned more about Leila's work with Elias Vale. He is Leila's widower and Mara's father, works as a records officer/cataloguer, and knew only that Leila had consulted with Vale on scientific work without knowing the full details. He knows Leila's warnings were read but deferred as politically inconvenient, and knows the archive's power supply is unstable. He possesses council-record folders and his archive maintenance coat. He is thin, grieving, protective, worried, and troubled by his failure to tell Mara about Leila's connection to Vale.

set.name: Elias Vale
set.description: Elderly physicist-philosopher and leader of the Continuance Project, currently at the Greenwich headquarters after showing Mara and Tayo the probe systems and archive preparations. He wants the probe to carry an honest record rather than a triumphant declaration and believes Mara's inherited distrust of official explanations makes her capable of writing it; he now accepts Tayo as a useful observer of the project's security and institutional weaknesses. He is connected to Leila through her fourteen months of work on the probe's trajectory, risk review, and ethical objections, and recruited Mara despite lacking certainty that he can protect her text from institutional editing. He knows the probe is designed to travel beyond the solar system and return in approximately eight million years, and understands the project may be captured by sponsors including the Meridian Union. He possesses a black composite cane, the draft writing agreement, authority within the facility, and access to the project systems. He is physically frail, intellectually alert, candid about compromise, and quietly determined.

set.name: Tayo Okafor
set.description: Mara's closest friend, currently at the Greenwich Continuance headquarters with her after obtaining a youth technical-consultation visitor pass. He is skeptical of institutions and security systems but intrigued by the probe's architecture, archive layers, audit protections, and isolated devices; he has begun investigating whether testimony and other project data can be edited without meaningful accountability. He listens closely, notices what people avoid saying, and writes code. He is Mara's trusted friend and now an informal technical ally to Vale and the project, though he does not trust its sponsors. He surrendered his tablet, earbuds, and ceramic multitool at security and currently possesses only his identity band. He is physically safe, alert, dryly humorous, and increasingly suspicious.
Mara tells Tayo about the Continuance Project, and he obtains a youth technical-consultation visitor pass to accompany her into Greenwich headquarters.

Mara learns that the Continuance archive will carry environmental and historical data, biological and genomic materials, seeds and cultures, language recordings, images, music, testimony, and models of extinct habitats alongside her text.
Tayo notices that the archive's testimony layer and audit protections may be vulnerable to institutional control, beginning his interest in investigating the project's security.
Tayo will investigate unexplained changes and unauthorized access in the Continuance archive and probe systems.
Mara will interview international witnesses and gather testimonies, recordings, and other materials for the archive.

chapters.name: A Vessel for the Future
chapters.content:
The next morning, Vale sent for Mara before the city had finished rationing its light.

A message appeared on her isolated phone at 06:12, bearing no signature and no greeting: OBSERVATION DECK. BRING THE KEY.

She read it twice beneath the grey window of the Venn flat. Adrian was asleep in the adjoining room, or pretending to be. Since the flood-barrier alert, he had begun sleeping in fragments, waking whenever the pumps changed pitch. The apartment’s emergency battery gave the kitchen a weak blue glow. In that colour, the brass key looked almost black, its chipped tag like a piece of painted sky.

Mara put it in her pocket beside Leila’s altered wool jacket. The jacket had belonged to her mother before it belonged to memory: one sleeve resewn, the collar rubbed pale, a small burn mark near the cuff from some laboratory heater. Mara wore it despite the warmth of the season. It smelled faintly of dust and the medicinal soap Adrian used on the archive’s paper gloves.

At the door she paused.

Adrian appeared in the hallway, thin in his old maintenance coat. “Greenwich?”

“Yes.”

“Did he say why?”

“Observation deck. Bring the key.”

Adrian’s eyes went to her pocket. He did not ask which key. “Don’t let them keep you there all day.”

“They have food.”

“That isn’t what I mean.”

“I know.”

He reached to straighten the jacket collar, then stopped before touching it. “Your mother hated heights.”

“Why are you telling me?”

“I don’t know.” He looked toward the sleeping room. “Maybe because people make plans for eight million years and forget the person standing beside them is frightened of a lift.”

Mara almost smiled. “I’m not frightened of lifts.”

“No. You’re frightened of what they carry you toward.”

Outside, London had been washed clean without becoming clean. Rain shone on the pavements, carrying soot into the drains. The elevated roads hummed with delivery vehicles, and beneath them people queued for the morning air stations. At the crossing, a public screen displayed the Continuance Project’s emblem: a white line curving around a dark sphere.

PRESERVE WHAT WE BECOME, it said.

Mara thought of Tayo’s voice. Institutions always want a voice when they mean a mouth.

At Greenwich, her band opened the inner gate. Tayo was not waiting by the lift. She felt an unreasonable disappointment until Vale emerged from a side corridor, tapping his black composite cane against the floor.

“Mr Okafor has been detained by a disagreement with our network engineers,” he said.

“Is he in trouble?”

“Not yet. He regards ‘not yet’ as a category of trouble.”

Vale led her through the headquarters to a service lift. It descended farther than the level she had seen yesterday. The walls were unpainted here, ribbed with old concrete and new conduits. A smell of oil replaced the sterile cold of the archive rooms.

“Why the key?” Mara asked.

“Because I want to show you the machine as it is, not as it is presented.”

“That sounds like a warning.”

“It is an invitation to distrust me accurately.”

The lift opened onto a platform suspended above the construction chamber.

Mara stopped.

The probe filled the cavern below them. Yesterday, seen through glass and distance, it had seemed like a dark animal. Now she could see its scale. It was longer than a city bus and narrower than a train carriage, assembled from nested shells of ceramic, titanium, carbon lattice, and a dull material that absorbed the chamber’s light rather than reflecting it. Its forward end tapered to a blunt shield. At the rear, folded instruments and antennae lay within protective vanes. Scaffolds surrounded it, crowded with workers in white and rust-coloured suits.

No one spoke loudly. The chamber had the hushed intensity of a hospital where the patient was too large to wake.

“The outer shell is sacrificial,” Vale said. “Micrometeoroids, dust, radiation. It will be damaged. We assume damage. The question is where we permit it.”

He pointed with the cane. Sections of the shell overlapped like scales. Under them ran a second skin of conductive mesh, then pressure compartments, then the archive vault.

“Nothing important has a single wall,” he continued. “Nothing important has a single copy.”

“Except the message.”

“Your message will be copied into every memory crystal.”

He handed her a transparent case. Inside lay a shard no larger than her thumbnail, colourless until she tilted it. Then blue and gold light moved through its edges.

“Memory crystal,” he said. “Fused silica with layered defects arranged as storage sites. We write in several physical orientations. A particle strike may erase a line in one layer and leave the others untouched.”

“Several copies?”

“Forty-eight complete copies. Twelve are active. The remainder are dormant, sealed against heat, radiation, and our own impatience.”

“Why forty-eight?”

“Because forty-seven seemed arrogant.”

She looked down into the chamber. “And if all of them are wrong?”

“Then the future receives an error with excellent redundancy.”

They crossed the platform to a control gallery. A schematic covered one wall, not as a straight route but as a tangled curve looping through the solar system and beyond. Coloured points marked the planets. Thin arcs bent around them, each turn stealing or lending velocity.

“This is the route,” Vale said.

Mara followed the line. It passed near Earth, swung around Venus, returned toward the outer planets, then vanished beyond the display’s edge. Another arc showed it coming back after a black interval.

“It doesn’t go straight.”

“Straight is expensive. Gravity is free, if you are willing to wait.”

He enlarged the diagram. “The probe leaves on a solar escape trajectory. It steals momentum from a sequence of planetary flybys and from the Sun itself. The route carries it beyond the heliopause, through the dark between systems. At the appointed interval, the clock releases a stored correction. The probe falls into a long return arc—not toward the Earth we know, which will not exist, but toward the calculated barycentric region where Earth’s descendants, ruins, or atmosphere may still offer a target.”

“Eight million years is an appointed interval?”

“Approximately. Celestial mechanics is not a promise; it is an argument with uncertainty.”

The display showed a cloud of possible returns, widening across the coordinates of a changed planet.

“What if it misses?”

“It probably will.”

Mara turned. “Then why build it?”

“Because missing is not the same as meaninglessness.”

“That is something people say when a plan fails.”

“Your mother said it was something people say when they want failure to sound noble.”

The words struck with the intimacy of an intrusion. Vale saw it and looked away.

“Leila objected to the route?” Mara asked.

“To the confidence with which we described it. She calculated the uncertainties more severely than the board preferred. She wrote that our return would be an act of statistical vanity if we pretended the destination was guaranteed.”

“Did you listen?”

“Sometimes.”

“Only sometimes?”

“I was less wise then.”

“Are you wise now?”

“No. Now I am old enough to recognize the shape of my mistakes.”

A technician opened a hatch beneath the probe’s central body. Vale guided Mara down a staircase to a smaller chamber. Here the walls were lined with the memory crystals, each sealed in its own dark frame. Their surfaces gave off no light. They seemed like pieces of frozen night.

At the centre stood the clock.

It was not digital. It had no glowing numbers, no screen, no obedient line of code. Brass wheels turned behind a transparent shield. A pendulum, short and heavy, moved with a deliberate tick. Ceramic teeth engaged one another with a soft, grinding patience. The mechanism sat inside three concentric cages, each isolated from the others by springs and fluid dampers.

“Mechanical?” Mara said.

“Partly. A crystal oscillator corrects the rate, but the counting is mechanical. We wanted a system whose failure could be seen.”

“By whom?”

“By anyone who opens it.”

“Eight million years of ticking.”

“Not continuously. That would exhaust every reasonable material. It sleeps through cycles, wakes to compare its drift, and sleeps again. The mechanical counter marks the elapsed intervals. There are independent clocks, each ignorant of the others until a scheduled check.”

“Again, copies.”

“Always copies.”

She watched the pendulum swing. Its sound entered her body more deeply than the machinery above. Tick. A pause. Tick.

“What happens when it wakes?”

“It checks the route. It wakes the archive. It unfolds the antenna. It transmits toward the return region.”

“And if there’s no one there?”

“Then it sends into silence.”

“Does that make you sad?”

Vale rested both hands on his cane. “Sadness is not a useful engineering specification.”

“That wasn’t what I asked.”

His face changed, losing its public patience. “Yes.”

They stood beside the clock while workers moved beyond the glass.

“The project’s first drafts began with ‘We, humanity—’” Vale said. “It was meant to sound generous. Universal. It sounded to Leila like a forged signature.”

“It is a forged signature.”

“Then do not use it.”

Mara looked at the dark crystal cases. “What am I supposed to write? ‘Some of us’? That sounds evasive.”

“Good.”

“Good?”

“Evasion can be dishonest. It can also be the first admission that a simple answer would be a lie.”

“You want me to say humanity was divided.”

“I want you to show it. Do not speak for a unified species. There was no unified species when we built this, and there will be no moral unity merely because a machine carries our nouns into the dark.”

“People will call that shame.”

“Some will. Others will call it treason. The frightened often confuse a description with an attack.”

“You’re asking me to put every conflict in the message.”

“I am asking you not to erase conflict in order to make the message beautiful.”

“And if the future judges us?”

“Let it judge us with evidence.”

The answer made her angry. It was too close to what she wanted and too close to the way adults had spoken about Leila: evidence, models, projections, acceptable uncertainty. Her mother had brought charts to council rooms and returned with the knowledge that charts could be filed while water kept rising.

“My mother died because officials deferred her warnings,” Mara said. “You know that.”

“I know.”

“You put her work into a machine and ask me to make it meaningful.”

“No.” Vale’s voice was quiet. “I ask you not to make it consoling.”

He led her back upstairs to the observation room. Tayo was there, seated beside the sealed recorder, arguing with an engineer whose expression had become professionally blank.

“Your friend has discovered that the audit system logs access but not the reason for access,” Vale said.

“I discovered it was designed by someone who thinks a timestamp is a conscience,” Tayo replied.

The engineer folded his arms. “The system meets all current standards.”

“Current standards are how the future inherits our excuses.”

Vale nodded toward the desk. “Begin.”

Mara sat. The paper was heavier than ordinary paper, fibred against damp and heat. At the top of the first sheet, the project had printed a heading in dark blue:

MESSAGE TO THE RETURNING WITNESS.

She crossed it out.

Tayo leaned over. “That’s a strong opening.”

“It assumes they’re a witness.”

“Maybe they’ll be nosy.”

“Maybe they’ll be nothing like us.”

Vale stood by the opaque glass. “Then write for the possibility that your reader is not an answer to your question.”

Mara held the pen above the page. She thought of Adrian waking to pump-noise. Of Leila’s jacket, its burnt cuff. Of the eastern gates shifting behind their concrete walls. Of the clock below them, counting not toward salvation but toward whatever survived the distance.

She wrote:

I am writing after a death, though not only my mother’s.

The sentence looked small. It did not explain anything. It did not ask to be forgiven.

She continued.

Grief is evidence. It proves that something was present, that a life altered the shape of other lives, that loss is not made harmless by the stories we tell about it. Do not take our grief as consolation. We often used consolation to avoid responsibility.

Her hand began to ache. She did not stop.

There were many of us. We shared a planet without sharing danger, power, language, or the consequences of our choices. Some warned. Some profited. Some obeyed. Some were trapped inside decisions made before they were born. We called all of this “we” because the word was convenient.

Tayo said nothing now. Even the engineer had turned toward the page.

Mara looked through the glass at the probe’s divided body. Every shell had been built to endure a different violence. No single surface could claim to be the vessel. No single voice could claim to be the species.

She wrote one final line before setting down the pen.

If you find us, begin with the disagreements. They are where our truth was hardest to destroy.

The mechanical clock ticked somewhere below.

Vale read the page from the doorway. His face did not brighten. That relieved her.

“Will you keep it?” Mara asked.

“For now.”

“No edits.”

“No edits by me.”

“That isn’t the same promise.”

“No,” Vale said. “It is the only honest one I can make.”

Tayo lifted the sealed recorder. “Then we’d better find out who else has access.”

Beyond the observation room, the probe waited inside its scaffolding, patient as a buried thought. Its route had been calculated through gravity, its memory divided against erasure, its clock built to outlast every hand that had touched it.

Mara placed Adrian’s key beside the page. The chipped blue tag touched the paper’s edge.

For the first time, the future did not feel like a promise. It felt like a room in which someone might eventually discover what had been hidden there.

set.name: Mara Venn
set.description: Seventeen-year-old writer, currently in the observation room at Greenwich Continuance headquarters after touring the probe with Elias Vale and Tayo Okafor. She is beginning the project’s message and has written opening notes describing grief as evidence, rejecting consolation, and refusing to speak for a unified humanity; she wants the record to preserve disagreement and responsibility rather than praise. She knows the probe’s long gravitational route is uncertain, its archive is protected by redundant memory crystals, and its timekeeping relies on a mechanical clock with independent checks. She remains Adrian’s daughter and Leila’s bereaved child, and knows Leila worked with Vale for fourteen months on trajectory, risk review, and ethical objections. She possesses Leila’s altered wool jacket, Adrian’s brass archive key with chipped blue tag, isolated registered phone, signed writing agreement, headquarters identity band, and first handwritten notes. She is physically safe but emotionally raw, distrustful of institutional promises, and newly committed to an honest, non-unified account.

set.name: Adrian Venn
set.description: Mara’s father, currently at their London flat while the municipal archive remains closed after the eastern flood-barrier alert. He wants to protect Mara and preserve records without provoking authorities, knows she is writing for the Continuance Project, and worries about the danger of the headquarters shaping or containing her. He is Leila’s widower and Mara’s father, works as a records officer/cataloguer, and knows Leila’s warnings were read but deferred as politically inconvenient, though he did not know the full extent of her work with Vale. He possesses council-record folders and his archive maintenance coat. He is thin, grieving, protective, sleep-deprived, and troubled by his failure to tell Mara about Leila’s connection to Vale.

set.name: Leila Venn
set.description: Deceased climate researcher and Mara’s mother, present through memory, archived documents, her council-hearing recording, technical warnings, and Vale’s account. She warned that barriers alone were not a plan and that managed retreat had to begin before the water chose for London; she was dismissed or deferred by officials. She worked with Elias Vale for fourteen months on the probe’s trajectory, risk review, and ethical objections, opposing triumphant language and arguing that a message beginning with ‘We’ concealed a crime. Her altered wool jacket, handwritten notes, technical warnings, and recording remain connected to Mara and the municipal archive. Her death from respiratory failure during the particulate emergency continues to shape Mara’s anger and her refusal to turn grief into consolation.

set.name: Elias Vale
set.description: Elderly physicist-philosopher and leader of the Continuance Project, currently at Greenwich headquarters after giving Mara a private tour of the probe and urging her to write without pretending humanity is unified. He wants an honest record that preserves conflict, evidence, and responsibility rather than a consoling declaration, but admits he cannot guarantee that institutional actors will not edit the work. He is connected to Leila through her fourteen months on the probe’s trajectory, risk review, and ethical objections, recruited Mara because of her inherited distrust, and accepts Tayo as an informal security observer. He knows the probe’s gravitational route may miss its future target, its archive has forty-eight redundant memory copies, and its clock uses mechanical and independent systems. He possesses a black composite cane, authority within the facility, access to project systems, and Mara’s opening page. He is physically frail, candid about his past mistakes, intellectually alert, and quietly determined.

set.name: Tayo Okafor
set.description: Mara’s closest friend and technical ally, currently at Greenwich headquarters in the observation room after helping inspect the project’s access controls. He is skeptical of institutions and sponsors, listens for what people avoid saying, writes code, and has discovered that the archive audit system records access timestamps without recording the reasons for access; he intends to investigate whether files can be changed without meaningful accountability. He is Mara’s trusted friend, an informal ally to Vale, and a wary observer of the project. He surrendered his tablet, earbuds, and ceramic multitool at security and currently possesses only his identity band and a sealed recorder. He is physically safe, alert, dryly humorous, and increasingly suspicious of the project’s security architecture.

Vale gives Mara a detailed tour of the probe’s nested protective shells, gravitational flyby route, redundant memory crystals, and independently checked mechanical clock, explaining that the return is uncertain rather than guaranteed.
Vale tells Mara not to speak for a unified humanity, and Mara writes her first notes defining grief as evidence and identifying conflict, unequal power, and responsibility as central to the message.
Mara will preserve and expand her opening notes into a message built from conflicting testimonies rather than a unified declaration.
The project’s access and audit systems will become subjects of Tayo’s continuing investigation for unexplained edits or unauthorized changes.

chapters.name: The First Voices
chapters.content:
The interviews began with a queue.

Not a queue arranged by the Continuance Project, though the project had provided the room, the chairs, the water allotments, and the numbered cards. The queue had formed outside the headquarters before Mara arrived, spilling beneath the rain awning and along the old maritime museum wall. People stood in coats that had dried stiff with salt, in work trousers marked with barrier grease, in school uniforms altered for heat. Some held folders. Some held photographs. Most held nothing, which made them look less prepared and therefore less likely to be believed.

A woman at the front was arguing with a receptionist.

“I was told I could speak for my building,” she said.

“You may speak about your experience,” the receptionist replied. “The archive cannot accept delegated testimony.”

“My building has three hundred people.”

“Then three hundred people may apply.”

Mara stopped under the awning. Tayo, beside her, made a small sound through his nose.

“Three hundred applications,” he said. “Efficient.”

The woman heard him. “You laughing?”

“No. I’m counting the ways this can go wrong.”

“That takes less time than applying?”

“Usually.”

The receptionist glanced at Mara’s headquarters band, then at the woman’s number. “Interview rooms are limited. We have to preserve comparability.”

Mara looked through the glass doors. Inside, the project’s emblem floated on every screen: a white line curving around a dark sphere. The line had the calm, inevitable shape of a thing already decided.

“Who chose the questions?” Mara asked.

The receptionist’s expression tightened. “The interview framework was developed by the Ethics and Representation Committee.”

“Who is on it?”

“I don’t have that information.”

Tayo leaned toward Mara. “First voice of the day: the person who isn’t authorized to know.”

The receptionist heard that too. “You’re here as technical consultation.”

“I’m aware. It’s printed on my band.”

Mara took the woman’s number. “Come with us.”

The receptionist opened her mouth, but Vale’s authorization appeared on the desk display before she could use it. ROOM THREE, it read. PRIORITY WITNESS.

The woman followed them inside without thanks.

Her name was Nkiru Bell, and she had lived in a twelve-storey block near the eastern gates until the evacuation sirens sounded two weeks earlier. The building had not flooded. That was the reason she had been denied emergency accommodation.

“The water stopped four streets away,” Nkiru said, sitting beneath the room’s soft recording light. “The pumps held. Everyone congratulated the pumps. No one asked what it cost to keep them running.”

“Can you describe the evacuation?” Mara asked.

“I can describe not being evacuated.”

The recorder’s red point illuminated.

Nkiru told them about the lift that stopped working after the electricity ration began, about carrying her father down nine flights while the stairwell smelled of sewage. She told them that the residents had formed shifts to move elderly people through the streets when the transport authority cancelled the buses. She told them a private security vehicle had come to collect executives from the newer towers, passing the queue without slowing.

“Did anyone help?” Mara asked.

“Of course. That is the insulting part.”

Mara looked up.

“People helped each other. Neighbours, market sellers, two boys from the academy. Volunteers came with filters. The city sent a message telling us to remain calm. The message was not useless. It told us where the water was highest. But it did not tell us why our building had no backup power while the towers across the road had three generators.”

Nkiru folded her hands. “Put that in your future machine. We were not helpless. We were abandoned and resourceful at the same time.”

Mara wrote the phrase in the margin of her paper.

Abandoned and resourceful.

When Nkiru left, Tayo tagged the recording with her name, building, neighbourhood, date, and the words infrastructure failure, mutual aid, unequal evacuation. Then he added a second tag: speaker disputes project category.

“What does that mean?” Mara asked.

“She said the category was wrong.”

“She was a displaced resident.”

“She was a displaced resident who objected to being reduced to displacement. If we don’t record the objection, we’ll turn her into the category she resisted.”

Room Four held a flood worker named Pavel Soren, whose boots had been cleaned but not his hands. Fine black grit remained in the cracks around his nails. He sat beneath the same light and looked at it as though it were a surveillance device.

“Do you believe this probe will return?” Mara asked.

“No.”

“Would you like it to?”

“That depends.”

“On what?”

“Whether it comes back carrying a bill.”

Tayo glanced at her, amused despite himself.

Pavel had worked maintenance on the eastern barriers for eleven years. He described the gates as if they were animals with habits: the old hinge on Section C that groaned before a pressure shift, the sensor that lied whenever the air became too wet, the concrete seam where water appeared in a thin shining line.

“People think a barrier is a wall,” he said. “A barrier is a negotiation. Water pushes. We answer. It pushes somewhere else. Every answer moves the question.”

“What would you want future beings to know?” Mara asked.

Pavel considered this. “That the wall did not fail by itself.”

Mara waited.

“Materials failed. Budgets failed. Maintenance schedules failed. Engineers warned. Managers postponed. Ministers renamed the postponement resilience. The water did what water does. We did the rest.”

He leaned closer to the recorder. “But don’t make us sound noble because we worked there. Some of us took bonuses to sign inspection sheets we had not finished. Some of us stayed twelve hours past shift because we knew the next crew was short. Some did both. People are not one thing just because you want a clean lesson.”

The sentence entered Mara more sharply than the first notes she had written in the observation room. The project wanted a lesson, perhaps. So did she. A warning, a guilty government, a brave worker, an innocent future. All the parts could be placed in order and made to point toward meaning.

Pavel would not permit it.

At midday the queue had doubled. Headquarters provided nutrient bars, but several people refused them because the wrappers displayed a sponsor’s logo. Tayo took two and read the ingredients aloud in a solemn voice until Mara told him to stop.

“Organizing is hungry work,” he said.

“You’ve eaten three.”

“I’m preserving them for the archive.”

He had turned an unused consultation room into a temporary sorting station. Six screens showed waveform thumbnails. Every recording was copied to a local drive, a project drive, and a sealed recorder he had smuggled no farther than the security gate had allowed. The sealed recorder was not connected to anything. Tayo treated it as a small, stubborn animal.

“Why keep a copy that cannot be checked?” Mara asked.

“Because a system that can check everything can also certify a lie.”

“Vale said the archive has forty-eight copies.”

“Of whatever they decide to put in it.”

He pulled up the morning’s submissions. Nkiru’s interview sat beside a list of approved witness profiles. The list divided people into resident, worker, displaced person, educator, child, researcher, cultural representative, and public official.

“What’s wrong with it?” Mara asked.

“Look at the access requirements.”

She read. Applicants needed identity verification, a stable contact address, a statement of relevance, and—under a heading marked supporting materials—letters from recognized organizations, employers, schools, councils, or registered relief bodies.

“People without those can still apply,” she said.

“Yes. They go to secondary review.”

“How many secondary reviews are there?”

“Three slots this month.”

Mara stared at the screen. “That can’t be the whole project’s selection process.”

“It isn’t. It’s only the process for getting into the room.”

The next witness was a family from the temporary settlement at Canning Town: a grandmother named Saira, her daughter Huda, and Huda’s two children. The grandmother spoke first because the younger adults had been told, at different offices, that their records were incomplete.

“We moved six times,” Saira said. “The system says we have no stable address. It is correct. We are very stable in our instability.”

Huda gave a tired laugh. The boy beside her did not. He was perhaps eight, with a yellow raincoat and a plastic dinosaur missing one leg.

Mara asked what they had brought from their old home.

“Nothing that was ours,” Huda said. “The documents came in a pouch. The clothes came from a distribution centre. The children have memories, but no one accepts those as proof.”

The girl, Leen, raised her hand.

“This is not school,” Huda told her.

“I know.”

Mara leaned forward. “What did you want to say?”

Leen held out a folded sheet of paper. On it she had drawn a house balanced on enormous wheels. The wheels had windows in them. Above the roof, birds flew in a line.

“Is it your house?” Mara asked.

“It’s the next one.”

“Where will it go?”

“Anywhere the water doesn’t know yet.”

Her brother finally spoke. “That’s not how water works.”

“You don’t know everything.”

“I know the water goes everywhere.”

Saira touched the boy’s shoulder. “His name is Sami. He listens to the pumps at night.”

Mara looked at him. “What do they sound like?”

“Like they’re trying not to be afraid.”

No one spoke for several seconds. The recorder continued its quiet work.

Mara asked the family what a future being should receive from them. She expected food, a map, a warning, perhaps the names of officials who had refused their applications.

Saira said, “A recipe for lentils that can survive a bad year.”

Huda said, “The truth that leaving is not the same as choosing to leave.”

Leen said, “The house.”

Sami said, “A way to hear the pumps before they stop.”

Tayo marked each answer separately. He did not combine them under family testimony.

“Why not?” Mara asked later.

“Because they disagreed.”

“They’re a family.”

“Exactly.”

In the afternoon, Mara visited a primary school whose upper floors had become a cooling shelter. The children were interviewed in groups of four, with a teacher present and a project ethicist observing from behind the glass. The children had been invited to draw something they wanted preserved for eight million years.

Most drew animals. A fox with blue antlers. A whale floating above a city. A dog wearing a crown. One child drew a packet of crisps and wrote DO NOT OPEN UNTIL LUNCH.

“What did you draw?” Mara asked a girl named Priya.

“A door.”

“Why?”

“So someone can come in.”

“Who?”

She shrugged. “Someone who knows where we are.”

A boy named Marcus drew a timetable. “This is important,” he said. “If you don’t know when things happen, you can’t get ready.”

Another child, Amadou, objected. “Timetables change.”

“Then you write the changes.”

“Then it’s not a timetable.”

The children began arguing. The teacher tried to quiet them, but Mara lifted a hand.

“Let them continue.”

The argument grew more serious than the drawings deserved. A timetable meant safety to Marcus; to Amadou it meant a promise adults made and then blamed children for believing. Priya said a door was better because it did not tell you when to leave. A boy at the end of the table said a door was dangerous if it opened onto water.

The ethicist behind the glass tapped a note into her tablet.

“What?” Tayo asked when they rejoined him.

“Nothing,” Mara said.

“That is never what a person means when they say ‘what.’”

“She categorized the children’s disagreement as developmental.”

“Was it?”

“I don’t know.”

“Then don’t let her know for you.”

By evening Mara’s notebook had become crowded with phrases that refused to stand together neatly: abandoned and resourceful; the wall did not fail by itself; a house that moves; a door for someone who knows where we are; a recipe for a bad year. She had imagined that the future would value our greatest achievements—mathematics, music, the images sent beyond the atmosphere, proof that intelligence had once looked up and wondered.

But the people in the rooms had offered maintenance schedules, lentils, doors, pumps, and the right not to be summarized.

Tayo exported the recordings. A warning appeared on his screen.

UNVERIFIED SPEAKER CONSENT.

“Pavel signed,” Mara said.

“The system says his signature is not associated with an institutional credential.”

“He works for the barrier authority.”

“Temporary contractor.”

“Nkiru?”

“Address mismatch.”

“Saira?”

“Insufficient documentary continuity.”

Mara felt the room contract around her. “And the children?”

“School consent is valid. The school is registered.”

“So the children count because the institution can prove it owns the interview.”

Tayo looked at the screen. “That’s not what it says.”

“It doesn’t have to say it.”

He turned the monitor toward her. The approved recordings were marked in green. The others were amber, pending review. None was rejected yet.

“Can you copy the amber files into the archive?”

“Not without authorization.”

“Can you copy them somewhere else?”

“I already did.”

Mara looked at the sealed recorder.

Tayo nodded. “Their voices exist outside the project’s permission.”

“Is that safe?”

“No.”

“Is it legal?”

“Less safe.”

She thought of Vale’s warning: no edits by me was not the same as no edits. The interviews had begun as a search for what future beings might value. Now she understood that the first question was more immediate: who would be allowed to exist in the record at all?

Tayo closed the sorting window. “You should write down what happened today.”

“I’ve been writing all day.”

“Not the testimonies. The selection.”

Mara opened a clean page.

He dictated, not as an official statement but as a list: those with addresses; those with employers; those with recognized papers; those whose consent could be verified by an institution; those who waited outside; those whose voices were accepted only provisionally.

At the bottom, Mara added her own line.

A record can be accurate and still be unjust if the doorway is built for only one kind of person.

She underlined it once.

Outside, the floodlights came on over Greenwich. Beyond the glass, London darkened in pieces, neighbourhood by neighbourhood, as the rationing grid withdrew its light. In the distance, the barriers stood against the tide, immense and temporary.

Mara gathered the day’s pages. She had expected the first voices to tell her what humanity was. Instead they had shown her how many ways a person could be prevented from becoming evidence.

The future, she thought, would not need a single voice.

It would need to know who had been kept silent.

chapters.name: The Drowned Coast
chapters.content:
The first thing Mara noticed about Lagos was that the water had learned the streets.

It moved through them without hurry, occupying the gutters, the market entrances, the hollows beneath pedestrian bridges. In London, floodwater arrived as an emergency, announced by sirens and red bands on municipal screens. Here, in the wet season, it seemed less like an invasion than a second geography laid over the first. People crossed it in sandals. Children balanced along the raised edges of pavements. A woman selling phone batteries had built her stall on concrete blocks and kept her stock in a floating plastic crate tied to her wrist.

The Continuance shuttle descended through a ceiling of brown cloud. Beyond the window, Lagos spread in fragments: bright roofs, rusted roofs, towers with mirrored sides, lagoons stippled by boats, roads shining as though varnished. The Atlantic pressed against the city from the south. Mara could not see where one ended and the other began.

“Don’t make that face,” Tayo said beside her.

“What face?”

“The face of someone discovering that a crisis has a population.”

She turned from the window. He had been awake for most of the flight, watching the shuttle’s diagnostic display on the seat in front of him. His headquarters identity band blinked green. His sealed recorder was hidden in the inner pocket of his borrowed project jacket.

“I knew Lagos had flooding,” she said.

“You knew the word.”

The shuttle banked. A long strip of coast appeared below them, interrupted by seawalls, construction platforms, drowned foundations, and neighborhoods that seemed to have been assembled from whatever the previous flood had not carried away.

Mara opened her notebook. On the first page, beneath grief is evidence, she wrote: Water has a population.

Their escort from the Continuance Project was a compact woman named Bisi Adebayo, who had worked in Lagos’s coastal adaptation office until the office lost its independent budget. She met them at the landing field with a portable air monitor clipped to her collar and a scarf tied over her hair.

“Your lungs will complain,” Bisi said. “Ignore them only if you have to.”

“Is that official medical advice?” Tayo asked.

“No. Official medical advice is delayed until the procurement committee meets.”

She led them through the terminal, where fans pushed hot air from one end of the building to the other. The walls carried advertisements for Meridian desalination systems and a new inland city planned by a consortium whose logo appeared on half the public screens.

Mara stopped before a map of the coast. The old shoreline was drawn in blue. The current evacuation boundary was marked in orange. A third line, in white, indicated the zone expected to become uninhabitable within thirty years.

“Who made this?” she asked.

“Three universities, two ministries, and a company that owns the sensors,” Bisi said. “They disagreed about the dates. They agreed not to print the names of the neighborhoods likely to disappear.”

“Why?”

“Investors dislike being told where their future resorts will be underwater.”

Outside, heat struck Mara with the intimacy of breath. The city smelled of diesel, salt, fruit, wet concrete, and vegetation beginning to rot. Tayo lifted the air monitor’s spare readout from Bisi’s hand.

“Particulates are high,” he said.

“They are always high.”

“Your monitor says moderate.”

“It is calibrated for the ministry.”

He looked at her.

Bisi shrugged. “You asked for honesty. I’m giving you the local variety.”

The marine laboratory stood on reclaimed ground at the edge of the lagoon. Its lower level had been abandoned after a storm surge, and the old doors were furred with salt. New laboratories occupied the upper floors, connected by walkways to a floating platform where tanks of seawater rose and fell with the tide.

Amina Bello was waiting beside the largest tank.

She was younger than Mara expected, perhaps in her thirties, with close-cropped hair and a scar running from her left ear to the hinge of her jaw. A blue glove covered one hand. In the tank behind her, small silver fish moved around a branching structure of pale coral.

“Those are not wild colonies,” Amina said before Mara could ask. “They are survivors bred for heat tolerance. We took their eggs from a reef that no longer exists.”

Mara looked into the water. The fish turned together, a single thought breaking into many bodies.

“Will they survive?”

Amina’s mouth tightened. “That is the question people ask when they want a hopeful sentence.”

“I’m not asking for one.”

“Good.”

Amina waved them toward the tank. The water was cloudy near the bottom. A sensor arm recorded temperature, acidity, oxygen, and the presence of industrial compounds.

“Five decades ago, this coast had mangrove belts wide enough to slow storm water,” she said. “Then they were cleared for estates, ports, roads, and shrimp farms. Some were cut by local operators. Some were licensed by national authorities. Some were removed by international developers who promised employment and left behind a wall, a security road, and a pamphlet about sustainability.”

She tapped the glass.

“Every time a report said the mangroves were essential, someone replied that the economy could not wait for trees. The economy was always allowed to be urgent. The water was told to be patient.”

Tayo was recording on the project equipment. Mara noticed that Amina watched the red light with suspicion.

“Who will own this interview?” Amina asked.

“The Continuance archive,” Mara said.

“That is not an answer.”

Mara felt the familiar contraction in her chest, the sensation of a doorway narrowing. “I will submit the recording under your name. You can review the transcript.”

“Can I remove it?”

“Before the archive is sealed, I think.”

“You think.”

“The rules are still being defined.”

“Then write that the rules are still being defined. People speak as if an archive is a cupboard. It is not. An archive is a country with a border.”

Mara wrote the sentence down.

Amina showed them the specimens in the tanks: juvenile rays with damaged fins, oysters from a dead estuary, mangrove seedlings growing in perforated drums, a sea grass that had survived in a drainage channel beside an oil terminal. Each sample had a number, a collection date, a location, and a status.

One label read: EXTINCT IN WILD.

Another read: UNKNOWN.

“What does unknown mean?” Mara asked.

“That we have not found it alive, but we have not earned the right to call it dead.”

In a side room, Amina played recordings gathered from hydrophones. The first was the layered clicking of dolphins. The second was the low pulse of a distant engine. The third was almost silence, broken by a scrape and a burst of static.

“Before the shipping lanes expanded, the lagoon carried more voices,” Amina said. “Fish, crustaceans, mammals, insects. We measured some of them. We named some. We destroyed many without ever learning their names.”

Mara thought of the project’s list: biological and genomic materials, seeds and cultures, models of extinct habitats. It had sounded comprehensive in Greenwich, a great cabinet of life assembled against oblivion.

“Can the archive include the species?” she asked.

“Their tissue, perhaps. Their sequences. Their calls if someone recorded them. But not their consent.”

“No one’s consent is in the archive.”

“Exactly. Yet humans will speak in the first person and call it representation.”

Amina removed her glove. Her bare fingers were stained green at the tips.

“You must include what we destroyed,” she said. “Not only what we loved. The reef that became a shipping channel. The wetland drained for a city that was advertised as safe. The fish poisoned by compounds whose manufacturers placed warnings in documents no ordinary person could read. Include the names of the agencies, the companies, the ministers, the banks. Species do not destroy themselves because the water became inconvenient.”

Mara hesitated. “Would naming them make the message an accusation?”

“It is an accusation.”

“Vale wants evidence.”

“Evidence of what? That a storm occurred? That coral bleaches? Future beings will know what happened to the coast. They may not know who signed the permits.”

The question followed Mara through the laboratory.

At noon they traveled by a narrow electric boat to a settlement beyond the old coastal road. The boat’s hull scraped plastic from the surface. Mangrove roots rose from the water like black fingers, but most stood among concrete pilings and collapsed fences. A boy in a red shirt waved as they passed. Behind him, an entire row of houses had sunk until only their upper windows remained above the tide.

The evacuation zone began where the road disappeared.

People lived on a chain of raised platforms connected by planks. The platforms had once been temporary. Bisi told Mara they had existed for nine years.

“Temporary is a political word,” she said. “It means no one has to budget for its ending.”

At a distribution point, women sorted water filters while a generator coughed beneath a tarpaulin. An elderly fisherman named Eze showed Mara a laminated photograph of the coast before the last great surge. He stood in it beside a canoe, one hand on the shoulder of a girl who might have been his daughter.

“The fish moved farther offshore,” he said. “Then the water became too warm. Then the nets came back with oil, or nothing. We were told to change professions.”

“Were you offered training?”

“They offered a lecture.”

He laughed without pleasure. “The lecturer had never touched a net.”

Amina had come with them. She asked whether Eze wanted his testimony recorded. He looked at Mara.

“Will the future eat fish?”

“I don’t know.”

“Then tell it we were here.”

He spoke for eleven minutes. He named the fishing grounds, the seasons, the dead mangroves, and the vessels that had discharged waste at night. He named a shipping company, a petroleum contractor, two ministries, and the local official who had told the fishermen to stop using the word poisoning because it damaged investment confidence.

When he finished, Mara asked what he wanted preserved.

“My daughter’s song,” he said. “She used to sing when we returned from the water.”

“Do you have a recording?”

“No. But I remember the first line.”

He sang it softly. The melody rose and fell like a small boat crossing uneven waves. Amina joined him on the second phrase. Bisi looked away.

Tayo lowered his recorder after the song ended. “Do you want that included?”

Eze frowned. “Why would I have sung it otherwise?”

The project form required explicit permission for music, separate from testimony. Tayo read the clause aloud. Eze listened, then pressed his thumb into the approval field.

“Make the form learn the song,” he said.

On the return journey, rain came down so hard the lagoon lost its horizon. Mara sat beneath the boat’s canopy, listening to the roof tremble.

“Add species,” she said.

Tayo glanced at her. “To the message?”

“Not as a list. As witnesses. Or victims. Or both.”

“Fish don’t testify.”

“Neither do the dead.”

“That has never stopped us.”

She looked through the rain at the submerged houses. “Amina says tissue and sequences aren’t the same as a life.”

“She’s right.”

“Then what can we send?”

“Proof that we knew.”

The answer was too simple, and therefore frightening.

Back at the laboratory, Amina gave Mara a packet sealed in clear polymer. Inside were three dried mangrove leaves, a small coral fragment, and a strip of cloth marked with sample numbers.

“These are duplicates,” she said. “The project has its own specimens.”

“Why give me these?”

“Because institutions lose things in orderly ways.”

Mara accepted the packet. “What should I write?”

Amina considered her for a long time.

“Write that the coast was not a tragedy without authors. Write that some people warned, some profited, some obeyed, some were trapped, and some helped each other while the water entered their homes. Write that the living world was not scenery behind human history. It was the condition of history.”

Mara placed the packet beside Leila’s altered jacket in her travel bag. The leaves clicked softly against the coral as the boat rocked at the dock.

Before they left, Amina stopped her.

“You wrote something in your notebook when you arrived.”

Mara looked down. “Water has a population.”

“Good. Don’t make the population decorative.”

That night, in the project quarters, Mara listened through headphones to Eze’s song and the hydrophone recording of the vanished reef. Tayo sat on the floor with his back against the bed, copying files into his sealed recorder and a second device he had assembled from permitted components.

On her screen, the interview form asked her to classify the day’s material.

DISASTER TESTIMONY.
ECOLOGICAL LOSS.
CULTURAL MEMORY.
POLICY FAILURE.

Mara selected none of them. She opened a new field and typed the names Amina had given her: the developers, contractors, ministries, financiers, and officials. Then she added the names she did not know—the species never catalogued, the workers never paid, the families moved beyond the boundary of useful statistics.

The system warned: FREE-TEXT ADDITION REQUIRES REVIEW.

She saved it anyway.

In the margin of her notebook, beneath the words abandoned and resourceful, she wrote a new sentence:

The future must not be allowed to mistake consequences for weather.

Outside, rain covered Lagos. It struck the roofs, the platforms, the laboratory windows, and the dark water where the mangroves still held the soil together. Mara imagined the probe crossing its cold route beyond the planets, carrying forty-eight copies of whatever humans chose to admit.

For the first time, she understood that a message could fail without being lost. It could arrive perfectly and still conceal the hands that had made the world it described.
