She is angry, steady, defiant, emotionally shaken by Shen’s admission about Leila, and aware that Meridian may review her access.

set.name: Adrian Venn
set.description: Mara’s father currently in their London flat while the municipal archive remains closed and monitored during flood-barrier and Union security conditions. Shen has investigated him and offered Mara a protected municipal archive transfer and restored pension in exchange for editorial influence, though Adrian does not yet know the details of this offer. He has admitted that Leila calculated the probe’s return route and exchanged technical and ethical warnings with Vale about governments suppressing climate evidence. He possesses council-record folders, his archive maintenance coat, and surviving offline correspondence from Leila and Vale. He wants to protect Mara and preserve records, but recognizes his earlier silence as cowardice mixed with love. He is thin, grieving, sleep-deprived, fearful of archive surveillance, and vulnerable to Meridian administrative pressure.

set.name: Tayo Okafor
set.description: Mara’s closest friend and technical ally currently in the Kyoto institute lower archive after waiting outside and monitoring Mara’s private meeting with Shen. He continues preserving parallel copies of original and altered participation-safeguard records, including a fifth copy delivered to Chiyo. He heard enough of Shen’s offer to understand that Meridian launch access, security, and personal protections are conditional on editorial influence, and he knows the Meridian launch authority may review Mara’s access. He trusts Mara and respects Chiyo, remains skeptical of Vale, Shen, and all administrators, and uses humor to manage fear. He possesses the permitted backup device, cable kit, independent copies, copied participation-safeguard records, and the record of Shen’s offer. He is exhausted, tense, technically focused, protective of Mara, and alert to retaliation.

set.name: Chiyo Arai
set.description: Kyoto archivist currently in or near the institute lower archive after receiving Tayo’s copied original and altered records and a fifth copy of those records from Mara. She now also has access to Mara’s preserved account of Shen’s editorial bargain and necessity argument. She wants to preserve records without allowing institutional diplomacy or Meridian power to become historical truth, and supports Mara and Tayo while remaining skeptical of all monument-making authorities. She is physically composed, observant, authoritative, and quietly prepared for further archival resistance.

set.name: Shen Liao
set.description: Minister and principal advocate of the Meridian Union, currently in the Kyoto institute upper observatory after privately pressuring Mara. He sincerely believes centralized coordination is necessary because fragmented authority and delayed consent have produced famine, epidemic death, and preventable collapse. He acknowledges that the participation safeguard generalized suffering and erased responsible agencies, but argues that preserving diplomatic participation and immediate relief can justify compromised records. He offered Meridian-controlled fuel, shielding, navigation authority, communications security, launch protection, accelerated launch access, and personal protections for Adrian and Tayo in exchange for editorial influence and a context portraying the Union as the necessary culmination of human coordination. Mara refused his terms while agreeing to document both Meridian achievements and coercion. Shen knows Leila’s warnings, admits choosing centralized authority despite them, and recognizes that his emergency powers can become permanent. He is calm, strategic, disappointed rather than enraged, personally burdened by past epidemic deaths, and more dangerous because he believes domination can be a form of mercy.

Shen privately offers Meridian-controlled fuel, shielding, navigation, communications security, launch protection, and accelerated launch access in exchange for adding a coordination context that presents the Meridian Union as the culmination or necessary culmination of human coordination; he also offers protection for Adrian and Tayo’s record.

Mara rejects Shen’s bargain while agreeing to record the Meridian Union’s real improvements and coercive measures together, including rescues, prisons, restored watersheds, food routes, classified dead, and archive alterations.

Shen admits he knew Leila’s warnings and chose centralized authority because he believed distributed authority would continue killing people; he acknowledges that such authority is dangerous and that emergency powers tend toward permanence.

Mara creates a lower-archive file titled “THE LESSON OF NECESSITY,” preserving Shen’s argument that suffering must be controlled before it can be relieved and asking who controlled, benefited, and disappeared from the account.

Mara will preserve Shen’s offer and argument as evidence: Meridian launch access, security, and protection are conditional on editorial influence, while the Union’s genuine rescues must be recorded alongside coercion, classified dead, and controlled suffering.
The Meridian launch authority will review Mara’s access after she refuses Shen’s editorial terms, increasing institutional pressure on her and Tayo.

chapters.name: A Message for No One
chapters.content:
By morning, the rain had stopped, but the Kyoto institute still smelled of wet stone and overheated wiring.

The plenary chamber had been rearranged overnight. Rows of delegate desks faced a circular platform, and above the platform hung a projection of the probe: silver, incomplete, turning slowly in darkness. Its dimensions were displayed beneath it in six languages, as if size could be made reassuring by translation.

Mara arrived with Tayo and found that three desks had been removed.

“Who left?” Tayo murmured.

A clerk passing with a stack of tablets answered without looking up. “The Andean Coalition. The Pelagic Federation. The Northern Faiths Council.”

“Those are not small delegations,” Mara said.

“They are observing remotely.”

Tayo glanced at the empty desks. “That’s what people say when someone has walked out.”

At the front, Celia Rusk was speaking to two security officers. She wore a dark green jacket and the expression of someone who had slept well because other people had made the difficult decisions.

Celia saw Mara and came toward her.

“You should sit in the author’s enclosure,” she said.

“Why?”

“Because the agenda concerns the message.”

“The agenda concerns who gets to alter it.”

Celia’s mouth tightened. “Not today.”

“Especially today.”

Tayo touched Mara’s elbow. He carried the backup device beneath his coat, though the institute had required all personal storage to be surrendered at the door. He had hidden it in the lining after Chiyo showed him a maintenance passage that bypassed the inspection arch.

Mara looked toward the empty desks again. Each bore a nameplate and a small green light indicating remote participation. The lights made the absences look authorized.

“Where are they?” she asked.

“Engaged in consultation with their communities.”

“Because the draft reduced them to disaster totals.”

“Because they objected to the statistical framework.”

“That’s the same thing.”

“No,” Celia said. “It is a technical disagreement.”

Mara felt Leila’s sentence rise in her mind: no one should say *we* until naming who speaks, who is included, and who pays for the sentence.

She took her assigned seat.

The chair of the session, an elderly engineer from the Pacific Rim, called the meeting to order. The first item was the hazardous inheritance clause, a section concerning weapons, industrial systems, autonomous machines, and biological methods that might be reconstructed by whoever received the archive.

A delegate from the Meridian Technical Directorate stood.

“The archive must distinguish knowledge from instruction,” he said. “We can preserve evidence of dangerous technologies without preserving operational pathways.”

“Who decides what is operational?” asked a woman from the Southern Ocean Assembly. “The same committee that decided a map of flooded islands was politically sensitive?”

“That is an unrelated matter.”

“It is exactly related. You want the future to know that we built fusion arrays, orbital elevators, pathogen models, and autonomous weapons. You want it not to know how those systems were used against people who objected to the governments controlling them.”

The Meridian delegate lifted a hand. “If we include complete weapons records, we may be sending an invitation to extinction.”

“Then include the people who refused to use them.”

“Names of refusal are not a safety protocol.”

“Neither is forgetting who held the trigger.”

The argument widened. A military historian proposed preserving weapons as sealed diagrams, accessible only after a sequence of ethical acknowledgments. A religious delegate objected that an ethical lock would presume one morality could judge another. A systems engineer replied that without a lock, the archive would be a loaded chamber aimed at an unknown future.

Mara watched the probe turn above them.

A loaded chamber. A sealed inheritance. A warning concealed inside a monument.

She raised her hand.

Celia noticed and shook her head almost imperceptibly.

Mara raised it higher.

The chair recognized her. “The author may comment.”

“I’m not sure what we mean by dangerous technology,” Mara said. “A weapon can kill people directly. A dam can kill people by deciding whose homes are expendable. A database can kill people by making them visible to a government. A medicine can save a city and also become a license to control movement.”

The Meridian delegate frowned. “Are you suggesting we include every technical dependency and political context?”

“I’m suggesting that danger isn’t stored inside objects. It is stored in relationships.”

“And how would you encode a relationship for beings who may not share our language, bodies, or forms of reasoning?”

“By not pretending a list of objects is neutral.”

The Pacific chair leaned toward his microphone. “Please propose wording.”

Mara looked at the draft on her screen. “For every preserved dangerous system, include who controlled it, who was excluded from its benefits, who was exposed to its risks, and who argued against its use. If those records are incomplete, say they are incomplete.”

A man from the Continental Security League laughed once. “That is not an archive. It is a trial.”

“No,” Mara said. “A trial has a verdict.”

The phrase unsettled the room. It was easier for them to fight over a verdict than to accept a record that kept asking questions.

The second dispute concerned religious language.

The Northern Faiths Council had submitted a passage describing humanity as a creature entrusted with the care of creation. The wording had been rejected by the scientific review panel, which called it unverifiable and potentially exclusionary. The Council’s remaining representative stood with a tablet in both hands.

“You have preserved songs, burial rites, star maps, and the equations by which we measured distance,” she said. “But you have removed the words by which millions understood obligation. You call this neutrality. It is not neutrality. It is a preference for the sacred language of institutions that call themselves secular.”

A computational anthropologist replied, “The archive cannot endorse a deity.”

“Neither can it endorse the absence of one.”

“An archive records claims. It does not affirm them.”

“Then record ours as claims.”

Mara thought of Chiyo’s warning: civilizations could sacrifice people and truth to preserve their continuity. Here, continuity wore different clothes. Each faction wanted the future to inherit its most flattering explanation of why it had lived.

A delegate from the Ecumenical Assembly rose. “We will not allow our communities to appear as irrational populations attached to a statistical record of violence. Our traditions fed the hungry, sheltered displaced people, opposed slavery, and preserved languages when states failed.”

“Your traditions also justified conquest,” someone answered.

“So did your constitutions.”

The chamber broke into overlapping voices.

Celia struck the table. “The message cannot become an inventory of every human contradiction.”

“Why not?” Mara asked.

“Because the probe has finite capacity.”

“Then say what was excluded.”

“We are not sending an apology.”

“No one asked for an apology.”

Celia turned toward her. “You keep treating omission as a moral crime when sometimes it is engineering.”

“Sometimes,” Mara said, “engineering is how a moral crime gets made invisible.”

The representative of the Northern Faiths Council removed her earpiece. “Our communities will not participate in a message that describes our dead as regional casualties and our living as demographic blocs.”

She placed the earpiece on the desk and left.

The green light beside her name went dark.

No one called her back.

The third dispute began with nonhuman life.

A biologist from the Meridian Biocultural Consortium presented a proposed classification: domesticated species, wild species, engineered organisms, and ecological systems. Each would receive a proportional archive allocation based on documented human dependence and extinction risk.

Amina’s coral fragment was in Mara’s pocket. She felt its hard, pale edge through the fabric.

“Proportional to human dependence?” Mara said.

The biologist looked irritated. “We need a principled method.”

“You’re measuring value by usefulness.”

“By relevance to the human record.”

“The human record caused the damage.”

A delegate from the Oceanic Restoration Authority spoke through a translator. “We cannot represent species that have no symbolic or linguistic submission.”

“Then represent the evidence of what happened to them,” Mara said. “The heat readings. The empty nesting grounds. The hydrophones where there used to be reef noise. Amina’s specimens.”

“Specimens are not testimony,” said the biologist.

“They are not decorative either.”

The translator paused before rendering that. Around the room, people shifted in their seats.

A woman from the African Coastal Network requested the floor. She did not use the official microphone. Her voice came from the open channel, distorted by distance.

“You ask whether fish can testify,” she said. “Ask the families who could no longer fish because the water had been poisoned, and then ask whether the poisoned water is only background. You want the future to see an empty reef and admire your restoration technology. You do not want it to see the companies that removed the mangroves before the restoration began.”

Celia interrupted. “The archive will include ecological data.”

“Data without authorship is another form of weather.”

Mara’s hand closed around the coral fragment.

The phrase moved through her like a current. She opened the author’s notes and typed it into the draft.

**Data without authorship is another form of weather.**

The Coastal Network representative continued. “Our delegation withdraws unless the names of the coastal authorities, financiers, and corporations are restored. We will not allow our communities to be represented as populations that suffered a rise in temperature.”

Her channel went silent.

One by one, the remaining green lights of the African coastal delegates vanished.

The chair called for a recess. No one moved.

Instead, a new document appeared on every screen: a consolidated table of affected populations, displaced populations, deceased populations, and contributors. It had been prepared by the participation office. Mara scrolled through it.

Lagos: 18.4 million displaced.
Jakarta: 9.1 million displaced.
Athens corridor: 2.7 million mobile persons.
Unnamed coastal communities: 31 million affected.
Unverified deaths: 4.6 million.

The numbers were clean. They had no voices attached to them. No Eze singing his daughter’s song. No Ratri saying that the word *moved* concealed a life being pushed from one place to another. No Sami asking why the future deserved dreams.

Mara stood so quickly her chair struck the desk.

“This is not a message,” she said.

The chamber quieted.

“This is an admission form. A census of pain prepared by people who will never have to answer the people counted in it.”

Celia’s face hardened. “The table is a coordination instrument.”

“It is what happened when you removed their names.”

“The names are incomplete.”

“Then preserve the incompleteness.”

“That would make the archive unreliable.”

“No. It would make the reliability visible.”

The chair asked everyone to remain orderly, but order had already become the subject under dispute.

A delegate from the River Kingdoms rose. “Our communities are not withdrawing because they reject the project. They are withdrawing because participation has become permission to be summarized.”

Another delegate added, “We were invited to contribute testimony and then told the testimony endangered diplomatic cooperation.”

A third said, “If our governments refuse to be named, we cannot sign on behalf of those they harmed.”

Celia looked toward Mara. “Is this what you wanted? A message no one can endorse?”

Mara looked up at the projected probe. Its polished shell reflected the room’s quarrels as tiny moving lights. It had been designed to travel beyond the solar system, to cross distances that made nations absurd. Yet every component had been assembled through permissions, contracts, exclusions, and guarded doors.

Maybe that was the truth of any monument. It rose above the ground and invited people to forget who had carried the stones.

She thought of the probe’s future audience. Eight million years from now there might be no humans left, or humans might have changed into something that would not recognize the word. The message might be opened by minds without grief, or bodies shaped for oceans, or descendants who regarded Earth as an abandoned experiment.

What did it mean to speak to no one?

Perhaps the imagined audience was a disguise. Perhaps they were writing for themselves: the privileged asking an unknown future to confirm that their choices had mattered. A monument built by those who controlled the materials, addressed to an audience they could invent and therefore never disappoint.

Tayo leaned close. “You’re doing the face.”

“What face?”

“The one where you decide whether to destroy a room.”

“I’m deciding whether the room deserves to be preserved.”

He glanced at the table. “That’s different.”

“Is it?”

Chiyo stood at the rear of the chamber. She had entered without Mara noticing, carrying no tablet, only a paper folder. She lifted it slightly. On its cover was a handwritten list of the representatives who had withdrawn.

Not numbers. Names.

Mara felt something in her settle.

She returned to the microphone.

“I will not write a declaration that says humanity speaks with one voice,” she said. “There is no one voice here. There are empty desks, revoked testimonies, protected institutions, and communities that have been reduced to totals because totals are easier to negotiate with.”

Celia said, “You are exceeding your mandate.”

“My mandate is to write the message.”

“Not to define humanity.”

“I’m not defining it. I’m refusing to pretend it has already defined itself.”

The chair asked for a motion. None came.

The Meridian technical delegate closed his tablet. “Without a unified text, the launch authority cannot certify the archive.”

“Then certify the disagreement,” Mara said.

“That is not a launchable object.”

“No,” she answered. “It is a record of what the object cost.”

For several seconds, only the ventilation spoke.

Then the River Kingdoms delegate began gathering his papers. The Oceanic Restoration channel remained dark. The religious representative’s desk was empty. Across the chamber, more green lights disappeared.

The probe continued turning overhead, serene and unreachable.

Mara took Sami’s drawing from her folder and laid it beside the consolidated table. The little house on wheels had been drawn with uneven black lines. Its roof garden leaned toward the sun. A hose curled from one side, absurdly delicate and necessary.

“Put this in the archive,” Tayo said.

“They’ll call it anecdotal.”

“Then put the word anecdotal next to it.”

Mara looked at the drawing. “And if they refuse?”

“Keep it.”

She placed the paper back inside her folder, beside Amina’s specimens, Leila’s warnings, and the list of forty-seven erased riot victims.

The meeting was suspended without agreement. Officially, it had been a procedural delay. The public summary would say that several delegations had requested further consultation regarding representational balance.

In the corridor, Mara watched administrators replace the chamber’s nameplates in their cases. The empty desks would be filled again before the next session, perhaps by people instructed to speak more carefully.

Celia stopped beside her.

“You have made the project impossible,” she said.

Mara thought of the probe beneath its scaffolding, of all the money and labor already sunk into its shining body.

“Maybe it was impossible before I arrived.”

Celia’s eyes flicked toward the folder. “You think contradiction is honesty.”

“I think a clean record is usually evidence that someone cleaned it.”

“Future beings will not thank you for giving them confusion.”

“They don’t owe us thanks.”

Celia had no answer to that. She walked away.

Tayo waited until she was gone. “So,” he said, “monument?”

Mara looked through the corridor glass at the probe. Work lights burned beneath it, illuminating ladders, cables, and workers in pale helmets. The vessel seemed enormous from this distance, yet strangely empty. A container waiting for a voice.

“A monument,” she said, “unless we show the scaffolding.”

“And if showing the scaffolding stops the launch?”

“Then at least no one can say it stood by itself.”

She opened the draft and added a new heading:

**WHO IS SPEAKING, AND WHO HAS LEFT THE ROOM**

Under it she wrote the names Chiyo had recorded. Then she added the missing names she knew, and a line for those she did not.

The future might receive the message. It might not. The probe might fail in the dark, or return to a world that had no use for human words. It might be found by beings who understood only the materials, not the grief pressed into them.

Still, Mara kept writing.

Not because anyone was waiting.

Because the absence of an audience did not absolve the speaker.

set.name: Mara Venn
set.description: Seventeen-year-old Continuance message writer currently in the Kyoto institute corridor after a suspended plenary session, with Tayo nearby and Chiyo having preserved a paper list of withdrawn representatives. She is continuing to draft the message despite delegates withdrawing over statistical summaries and institutional objections to contradiction. She has argued that dangerous technologies require records of control, exclusion, exposure, and dissent; that religious language should be recorded as attributed claims; and that nonhuman life must be represented through ecological evidence and responsible human actors. She now questions whether the probe is a monument built by privileged people for an imagined audience and has added the heading “WHO IS SPEAKING, AND WHO HAS LEFT THE ROOM,” recording names, missing names, and disagreement. She trusts Tayo, values Chiyo’s archival judgment, remains allied but wary with Vale, distrusts Celia and administrators, and understands Shen’s belief in controlled suffering. She carries Leila’s altered wool jacket, Adrian’s brass municipal-records key, Sami’s drawing, Amina’s ecological specimens, testimony copies, Vale’s altered-record inventory, checksum strings, the forty-seven erased riot victims, paper and digital originals and altered records, Shen’s document and THE LESSON OF NECESSITY file. She is angry, thoughtful, defiant, and newly doubtful that an audience or successful launch can justify the project.

set.name: Tayo Okafor
set.description: Mara’s closest friend and technical ally currently in the Kyoto institute corridor after the plenary was suspended without agreement. He bypassed the inspection arch using a maintenance passage and continues carrying the permitted backup device, cable kit, and independent copies of original and altered records. He heard the delegates’ disputes over dangerous technology, religious language, nonhuman life, and statistical erasure, and supports Mara’s decision to preserve names, contradiction, and the archive’s scaffolding. He trusts Mara and respects Chiyo, remains skeptical of Vale, Shen, Celia, and administrators, and uses humor to manage fear. He is exhausted, tense, technically focused, protective of Mara, and alert to retaliation and further access review.

set.name: Chiyo Arai
set.description: Kyoto archivist currently in the institute corridor or returning toward the lower archive after attending the suspended plenary. She carried a handwritten list of representatives who withdrew and gave Mara a non-statistical record of their names, helping preserve absences that official summaries disguise as consultation. She now has access to Mara’s account of Shen’s bargain, the copied participation-safeguard records, and the names and omissions emerging from the plenary. She wants to preserve records without allowing institutional diplomacy, Meridian power, or a clean summary to become historical truth, and supports Mara and Tayo while remaining skeptical of monument-making authorities. She is physically composed, observant, authoritative, and quietly prepared for further archival resistance.

set.name: Celia Rusk
set.description: Representative of the Meridian Biocultural Consortium currently leaving the Kyoto institute plenary corridor after the meeting was suspended without a unified text. She defended statistical tables, technical limits, diplomatic participation, and institutional control, and accused Mara of making the project impossible when Mara demanded that omissions, withdrawn communities, dangerous technologies, religious claims, and ecological responsibility remain visible. She knows the participation-safeguard records reveal politically asymmetric alterations and wants to retain sponsor and administrative authority over the archive. She possesses delegate channels, sponsor influence, and access to official summaries; she is composed, territorial, hostile, and increasingly unsettled by Mara’s refusal to let the probe appear self-made or universally representative.

At the Kyoto plenary, delegates fought over how to archive dangerous technologies, with Mara arguing that risk belongs to relationships of control, exclusion, exposure, and opposition rather than to objects alone.

Religious delegates withdrew after their traditions were treated as statistical or unverifiable material, while other delegates argued that spiritual claims should be recorded without being endorsed as universal truth.
Coastal and other representatives withdrew when the participation office reduced displaced and dead communities to statistical summaries without names, testimony, or responsible actors.
Mara added the heading “WHO IS SPEAKING, AND WHO HAS LEFT THE ROOM” to her draft and began recording withdrawn representatives, missing names, and unresolved disagreement.

Mara explicitly questioned whether the probe was a monument built by privileged institutions for an imagined future audience, deciding that any honest message must show the scaffolding of power and labor behind it.

Mara will preserve dangerous technologies with their controllers, excluded beneficiaries, exposed populations, dissenting voices, and incomplete safety context rather than treating objects as neutral.
Mara will include religious and spiritual interpretations as attributed claims without allowing any tradition to become the archive's universal authority.
Mara will include nonhuman ecological evidence and identify the authorities, corporations, financiers, and communities connected to both ecological destruction and restoration.
Mara will preserve the names of withdrawn representatives, empty participation, and unresolved disagreement as part of the message rather than presenting a unified human voice.

chapters.name: The Accusation
chapters.content:
The accusation arrived before breakfast, folded into the municipal news feed between a flood-barrier failure in the western districts and an advertisement for Meridian sleep medication.

Mara was in the Kyoto institute cafeteria with Tayo when every wall-screen changed at once.

The probe vanished. In its place appeared a photograph of Elias Vale, taken years earlier, his face enlarged until the lines around his eyes looked like cracks in a wall. Beneath it, a red banner read:

**CONTINUANCE LEADER ACCUSED OF ENGINEERING GLOBAL SHAME**

Tayo stopped with his spoon halfway to his mouth.

“Engineering,” he said. “That’s a word people use when they don’t want to say lying.”

The presenter spoke over footage of the previous day’s plenary: an empty delegate’s chair, the darkened green lights, Mara standing at the microphone. The image had been cut so that her sentence began halfway through.

“—refusing to pretend humanity has already defined itself,” she said.

The footage froze on her face.

The presenter continued. “According to documents obtained by the Meridian Civic Service, Dr. Vale selected an inexperienced student to author the Continuance message specifically because she could be directed toward an accusatory interpretation of human history. Observers say the project has been captured by a faction determined to shame entire populations rather than recognize the achievements that allowed civilization to survive.”

Mara felt the cafeteria tilt around her.

“That isn’t what happened,” she said.

“No,” Tayo replied. “But it has your face.”

The screen showed a second document. It was a scan of her appointment agreement, with the paragraphs concerning independent editorial judgment highlighted in yellow. The signature at the bottom had been blurred, though not enough to hide the shape of her name.

**MARA VENN: VALE’S CHOSEN MOUTHPIECE?**

A panel of commentators appeared. One was a Meridian historian Mara recognized from the official launch broadcasts. Another was a former security minister from the Continental League. The third was a woman introduced as a survivor of the old imperial famines.

The survivor spoke first.

“My grandparents were starved by borders drawn in rooms where no one had ever seen their fields,” she said. “We will not accept a new monument that turns our suffering into ammunition against ordinary people.”

Her anger was real. Mara heard it in the tightening of her breath.

The historian nodded gravely. “Exactly. The Continuance archive should preserve the dignity of civilizations, not invite future beings to condemn them according to the private resentments of a project leader.”

“Private resentments?” Tayo said. “Vale has spent forty years trying to get people to read records.”

The former minister leaned toward the camera. “Dr. Vale has always believed conflict is more truthful than cooperation. He has surrounded himself with young radicals and representatives who reject the very institutions making the launch possible. This is not scholarship. It is ideological sabotage.”

Mara put down her cup.

“Who gave them the agreement?”

Tayo was already opening his backup device beneath the table. “Not the institute. The scan has a Meridian relay watermark.”

“Can you prove that?”

“I can prove the file was re-encoded through three public channels and one channel pretending to be public.”

“That is not the same as proving who released it.”

“No. It’s the same as proving they wanted us to stop looking at the first channel.”

On-screen, the presenter introduced a live feed from outside the Greenwich facility.

The rain there was hard and silver. Thousands of people had gathered behind barriers along the river road, their signs bright under the municipal lamps.

**NO MORE EMPIRE IN THE NAME OF HUMANITY**

**OUR DEAD ARE NOT YOUR ARGUMENT**

**THE FUTURE DOES NOT BELONG TO VALE**

A woman in a yellow coat shouted into a street microphone that the project was another rich-world monument built from the wreckage of poorer nations. Behind her, a group held photographs of drowned villages and children who had died during the southern heat migrations. Their grief had not been manufactured. Even through the feed, Mara could feel its weight.

Then the camera swung toward a second crowd.

There were men and women in identical gray rain capes, all holding the same placard:

**MARA VENN SPEAKS FOR NO ONE BUT VALE**

Their chant began softly, then synchronized through the public-audio system.

“Return the message. Return the lie. Return the message. Return the lie.”

A girl near the barrier turned toward the camera, bewildered, while an automated caption assigned her the words **WE DEMAND ACCOUNTABILITY**.

Tayo enlarged the feed. “There. The chant is being generated under the crowd audio.”

Mara watched the gray capes move in perfect intervals. The people holding them were not all actors. Some looked angry; some frightened; some were simply following the loudest voice available.

A reporter approached the woman in the yellow coat.

“Are you protesting against the Continuance Project?”

“I’m protesting against the project pretending it can speak for those it has never protected,” the woman said. “My family lost land twice. Once to empire, once to the climate policies that empire made possible. If Vale wants to preserve history, he can begin by saying who owned the ships, who profited from the ports, and who was told to move.”

The reporter turned to the camera. “As you hear, critics say the project’s language risks reopening historical wounds.”

The woman shouted after her. “They’re not wounds if they’re still killing us!”

The feed cut back to the studio.

The presenter’s expression had become sympathetic. “The question now is whether one individual, chosen without public mandate, should be permitted to define the human record. The Continuance board is expected to meet today to discuss Dr. Vale’s authority.”

Mara looked at Tayo.

“They’re removing him.”

“They’re considering removing him.”

“Same thing, with better grammar.”

A message arrived on her institute tablet. It was marked **URGENT — INTERNAL DISTRIBUTION ONLY**.

All Continuance personnel were instructed not to engage with media, not to leave the Kyoto institute without authorization, and not to access project systems except for assigned duties. The statement concluded with a warning against “unauthorized amplification of divisive material.”

At the bottom was Celia Rusk’s name.

Mara pushed back from the table.

“Where are you going?”

“To find Vale.”

The institute had placed him in a restricted consultation room after the plenary. Two security officers stood outside it now. They did not stop Mara, but they did not move aside either.

“He is in a board call,” one said.

“Then tell him I’m here.”

“We have instructions.”

“From whom?”

The officer glanced at the camera above the door. “The institute.”

Tayo stepped beside her. “Does the institute include a name, or is it one of those institutions that speaks without a person attached?”

The officer’s jaw tightened.

Before the exchange could become a detention, the door opened. Vale stood inside with one hand braced against the table. His face looked older than it had the previous night. On the wall behind him, a dozen board members appeared in separate windows: Celia, two launch engineers, a Meridian legal adviser, a representative from the Pacific Rim, and Shen Liao in a dark room whose background gave no clue where he was.

“Mara,” Vale said. “Come in.”

The officers allowed Tayo through as well, perhaps because the board wanted witnesses or perhaps because nobody had decided what rules applied.

Celia’s image enlarged. “Dr. Vale, this is not an informal consultation.”

“Nor is a public accusation,” Vale said.

“You were asked to remain silent while the board reviewed the media report.”

“The report quotes documents released by your partner institutions.”

“Do not confuse Meridian media with the board.”

“I don’t. Meridian media is confusing the public on your behalf.”

One of the launch engineers looked down. The legal adviser said, “The issue is not the source. The issue is whether your conduct has compromised the project’s diplomatic viability.”

Mara felt heat rise in her throat. “By recording what delegates said?”

“By encouraging confrontational framing.”

“I did not encourage anyone to withdraw.”

“You gave them language with which to withdraw.”

Vale’s expression changed. “That sentence should be preserved exactly.”

Celia ignored him. “The public has been shown a pattern of hostility. You selected Mara Venn, a minor with no diplomatic mandate, and placed her at the center of an international process. Her interventions now appear to reflect your personal philosophy.”

Mara stared at the board windows. “I was selected because I’m seventeen?”

“No,” Vale said. “You were selected because you understand that a record can be true without being flattering.”

“That is precisely the problem,” said the legal adviser. “The project is not authorized to produce a hostile interpretation of humanity.”

“Who authorized a friendly one?” Mara asked.

No one answered.

Shen did. “The project was authorized to preserve cooperation among its contributors. If contributors withdraw, the archive loses material, access, and launch support.”

“You mean leverage,” Mara said.

“I mean conditions.”

“Conditions that change what can be remembered.”

Shen’s gaze settled on her through the screen. “You have mistaken exposure for courage. There are communities whose dead are being used by old powers to settle scores, and there are communities being asked to accept blame for decisions made before they were born. A message that names every crime without distinguishing inheritance from agency can become another weapon.”

Mara thought of the woman in yellow. “Then distinguish them.”

“I have asked you to do exactly that.”

“You asked me to place the Union at the end of history.”

“I asked you to acknowledge coordination as an achievement.”

“After you made it a condition of launch.”

Shen did not deny it. “Achievements can have conditions.”

Vale coughed. The sound seemed to travel through the room’s silence rather than interrupt it.

“The board is not deciding whether Mara is correct,” he said. “It is deciding whether truth that threatens participation is allowed to remain truth.”

Celia’s image flickered. “We are deciding whether you remain project director.”

There it was. The words had been waiting behind the accusation.

Mara looked at Vale. He had expected this, perhaps from the moment he first showed her the altered records. Yet expectation did not make him prepared. His fingers trembled against the table.

“What happens if you remove him?” she asked.

“The project continues under interim authority,” Celia said.

“With the current draft?”

“With a certified draft.”

“Meaning the Meridian version.”

“Meaning a version that can launch.”

Tayo gave a small, humorless laugh. “It’s amazing how often the future turns out to have a sponsor’s logo.”

The legal adviser spoke sharply. “Mr. Okafor, you are not a member of this board.”

“No. That’s why I can still hear you.”

For a moment, Shen almost smiled. Then the expression vanished.

Outside the room, the institute alarms began to pulse. Not the evacuation alarm. A communications alert. Every wall-screen in the corridor lit with a new headline.

**VALE’S STUDENT MOUTHPIECE REFUSES TO DENOUNCE ANTI-HUMAN AGITATION**

Beneath it appeared a photograph of Mara leaving the cafeteria, her face turned toward the screens. The caption identified her as “the minor author at the center of the Continuance destabilization.”

Her stomach dropped.

“How did they get that?” Tayo asked.

A second alert appeared. Someone had released a clipped recording of Mara saying, “Maybe it was impossible before I arrived.” The preceding exchange with Celia was gone. The clip was accompanied by an interpretation generated in six languages:

**MARA VENN DECLARES THE PROJECT IMPOSSIBLE AND CALLS FOR ITS DESTRUCTION.**

The officers outside the room reached for their tablets.

Vale closed his eyes.

“Mara,” he said quietly, “you need to understand what they are doing.”

“They’re making me responsible for your arguments.”

“They’re making me responsible for your anger.”

“And if they remove you?”

“Then they will say your anger proves I should have been removed.”

The board window filled with movement. Celia was receiving messages. The legal adviser leaned toward someone off-screen. Shen remained still.

Mara imagined the protest outside Greenwich: the real photographs, the automated chants, the people who had come because empire and climate violence were not abstractions to them; the gray capes, the copied signs, the manufactured certainty laid over genuine pain like a transparent sheet.

She understood then that disinformation did not need to invent anger. It only needed to separate anger from its cause, give it a convenient face, and point it where power preferred.

“I won’t denounce the protesters,” she said.

Celia looked up. “That is not what we asked.”

“You asked me to denounce agitation. The people outside are angry for reasons you helped erase.”

“And the people threatening staff?”

“Name them separately.”

“Everything cannot be separately named.”

“Then don’t call it a truthful record.”

Vale opened his eyes. Something steadier had returned to them, though his exhaustion remained.

“Record the accusation,” he told her.

Mara looked at him. “The one against you?”

“All of it. The broadcast. The protest. The genuine grievances. The fabricated captions. The board’s language. My role in creating the conditions for this project. Do not protect me by making the record cleaner.”

Celia stood in her window. “Dr. Vale, you are relieved of public-facing authority pending review.”

The sentence was delivered with administrative calm. A door closing without anyone admitting they had shut it.

Vale bowed his head once.

“Pending review by whom?” Mara asked.

“The board.”

“Which board?”

The Meridian legal adviser answered. “The certified Continuance authority.”

“That isn’t a name.”

“It is the authority recognized by the launch infrastructure.”

Shen finally spoke. “Mara, do not make this worse.”

She turned toward his window. “You mean do not make it visible.”

“No,” he said. “I mean do not let them use you as proof that every demand for control is justified.”

For the first time, his voice carried something like concern. It did not make him less dangerous. It made the danger intimate.

The call ended. The room returned to its ordinary dimensions: table, chairs, gray walls, a locked cabinet containing copies of the future.

Vale sank into a chair.

Tayo checked the corridor cameras. “They’ve restricted your access,” he said. “Mara’s too.”

“How restricted?” Mara asked.

“Not yet detention. More like the building has decided you’re contagious.”

Vale looked toward the wall-screen, where her photograph remained beneath the accusation.

“Celia will publish an official clarification by noon,” he said. “It will state that I acted outside the project’s consensus procedures and that you were encouraged to adopt an inflammatory framework.”

“Were you?”

“I encouraged you to tell the truth as you found it.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“No,” Vale said. “I have often mistaken my preferred form of truth for truth itself.”

Mara thought of Leila leaving him, of the sentence about no one saying *we* without naming who paid. Vale had asked her not to turn Leila into his doctrine. Now he was asking her to record his own failure alongside everyone else’s.

“Then I’ll record that,” she said.

He nodded.

Through the corridor glass, the projected image of the probe appeared again, rotating above the institute atrium. Its shell shone cleanly. Around it, workers moved through scaffolding, carrying tools and cables, their bodies briefly interrupting the light.

Mara opened her draft and created a new section beneath the names of the withdrawn delegates.

**THE ACCUSATION**

She wrote down the broadcast’s exact wording. She described the woman in the yellow coat and the photographs of drowned villages. She recorded the synchronized gray-capery chant, the false captions, the altered clip, and the way real grief had been recruited to carry an invented conclusion.

Then she wrote Vale’s name.

Not as the villain the broadcast required. Not as the innocent man he might prefer to become.

She wrote: **Elias Vale believed conflict must remain visible. He also built a project whose access depended on institutions that preferred agreement. He selected me, and selection is a form of power even when the selected person is allowed to disagree.**

Tayo read over her shoulder.

“That’s going to make him furious.”

“He told me to write it.”

“People say that until you do.”

Mara saved the file in three places: the institute account, Tayo’s concealed device, and an offline copy beneath the paper list Chiyo had given her.

Outside, a message appeared on the public screen.

**THE CONTINUANCE BOARD WILL MEET TO DETERMINE WHETHER DR. ELIAS VALE REMAINS FIT TO LEAD THE PROJECT.**

Below it, another line formed:

**MARA VENN HAS BEEN INVITED TO PROVIDE A STATEMENT.**

Tayo stared at it. “Invited?”

Mara felt the word settle over her like a net.

“Publicly identified,” she said.

Vale rose with difficulty. “Do not go alone.”

“I won’t.”

“Do not let them make you speak for me.”

“I won’t speak for anyone.”

The screens changed again, showing her name in larger letters.

Mara closed the draft. Her hands were shaking, but not from fear alone. Beneath the fear was an anger that no longer belonged to a single accusation, or a single man, or even the project. It belonged to the old trick of turning history into a weapon and then blaming the wounded for the blood on it.

The probe continued its patient rotation.

A monument, she thought, could be built from truth as easily as from lies if the people who built it decided they were entitled to the final shape.

She slipped Leila’s jacket closer around her shoulders, checked that Adrian’s brass key was still in her pocket, and followed Tayo into the monitored corridor.

Behind them, the door to Vale’s room locked with a soft mechanical click.

Ahead, the institute waited to hear what its chosen mouthpiece would say.

set.name: Mara Venn
set.description: Seventeen-year-old Continuance message writer currently in the Kyoto institute's monitored corridor after the board relieved Vale of public-facing authority pending review. Meridian media has publicly identified her as Vale's chosen mouthpiece and released altered clips portraying her as an anti-human agitator; she has been invited to provide a public statement. She has created a draft section titled “THE ACCUSATION,” recording the genuine grievances and manufactured disinformation surrounding the Greenwich protests, the board's language, and Vale's responsibility, including the power involved in selecting her. She remains committed to preserving contradiction, withdrawn voices, ecological authorship, dangerous technologies in context, religious claims as attributed claims, and visible editorial manipulation rather than speaking for a unified humanity. She trusts Tayo and values Chiyo, remains wary of Vale while accepting his demand that she record his failures, distrusts Celia and Meridian administrators, and recognizes Shen's concern as inseparable from his dangerous belief in control. She carries Leila's altered wool jacket, Adrian's brass municipal-records key, Sami's drawing, Amina's ecological specimens, testimony copies, Chiyo's handwritten withdrawal list, Vale's altered-record inventory, checksum strings, the forty-seven erased riot victims, paper and digital originals and altered records, Shen's document and THE LESSON OF NECESSITY file. She is frightened, angry, defiant, physically shaking but determined, and under increased monitoring with restricted institute access.

set.name: Adrian Venn
set.description: Mara's father currently in their London flat while the municipal archive remains closed and monitored during flood-barrier and Union security conditions. He possesses council-record folders, his archive maintenance coat, and surviving offline correspondence from Leila and Vale. set.name: Elias Vale
set.description: Elderly physicist-philosopher and Continuance Project leader currently in a restricted Kyoto institute consultation room after being relieved of public-facing authority pending board review. He admits that he selected Mara, that selection is a form of power, and that he has sometimes mistaken his preferred form of truth for truth itself. He has told Mara to record the accusation, the protests, and his own responsibility without protecting him through a cleaner account. set.name: Tayo Okafor
set.description: Mara's closest friend and technical ally currently in the Kyoto institute's monitored corridor with her after the public accusation and Vale's removal from public-facing authority. He retains the concealed backup device, cable kit, independent copies of original and altered records, and evidence that the media file was re-encoded through disguised public channels. He identified automated captions and synchronized audio in the Greenwich protest feed and continues protecting Mara while checking cameras, access restrictions, and possible retaliation. He trusts Mara and respects Chiyo, remains skeptical of Vale, Shen, Celia, and administrators, and uses humor to manage fear. set.name: Chiyo Arai
set.description: Kyoto archivist currently in or near the institute's lower archive after giving Mara a handwritten list of representatives who withdrew. She now knows the board has moved against Vale and that Mara has recorded the accusation and manipulated protest evidence. She remains prepared to preserve paper and independent records against institutional summary, supports Mara and Tayo, and remains skeptical of Meridian power and monument-making authorities. She is physically composed, observant, authoritative, and quietly preparing for further archival resistance under increased institute monitoring.

set.name: Shen Liao
set.description: Minister and principal advocate of the Meridian Union, currently participating remotely in the Kyoto board call from an undisclosed darkened location. He watched the board relieve Vale of public-facing authority and challenge Mara's framing, warning her not to let the accusation make every demand for control appear justified. He maintains that coordination, launch conditions, and protection can be achievements while acknowledging they carry conditions; he remains committed to Meridian influence over the archive and launch. He recognizes the danger of manufactured outrage but does not withdraw his support for centralized authority. He is calm, strategic, personally concerned but disappointed, and more dangerous because he believes control can prevent suffering.

set.name: Celia Rusk
set.description: Representative of the Meridian Biocultural Consortium and influential Continuance administrator currently participating in the Kyoto board call and directing institutional restrictions afterward. She supports the official claim that Vale encouraged confrontational framing, that Mara's selection compromised diplomatic viability, and that a certified version must preserve cooperation and launch access. She has helped impose media silence, monitoring, and restricted project access, while denying direct responsibility for Meridian media's release of altered material. She wants to remove Vale's authority, retain sponsor and administrative control, and prevent the archive from becoming an accusatory record. She is composed, territorial, hostile, and increasingly reliant on procedural language to conceal political choices.

Meridian media publicly accused Elias Vale of engineering global shame, portrayed Mara as his chosen mouthpiece, and released altered clips and captions to frame her refusal of a unified account as sabotage.

Protests gathered outside Greenwich, combining genuine anger over imperial and climate violence with synchronized gray-caped demonstrators, automated chants, and manufactured disinformation that redirected public grief toward Vale and Mara.

Mara created a draft section titled “THE ACCUSATION,” recording the broadcast, protest, manipulated media, Vale’s responsibility, and the power involved in selecting her as writer.

Mara will preserve the exact Meridian accusation, the genuine and manufactured elements of the Greenwich protests, and her own status as Vale's publicly identified mouthpiece in the message's record of power and editorial selection.
The Continuance board and Meridian launch authority will proceed toward removing Vale and replacing the unresolved message with a certified version that can launch under Meridian conditions.
